title: FAST-PETase, a machine-learning-engineered enzyme, depolymerised post-consumer PET and was reused by an independent lab
summary: A 3D-CNN ensemble engineered FAST-PETase, which degraded 51 post-consumer PET products in a week; Texas A&M later reported complete depolymerisation using it with MHETase.
account: In a paper published in Nature on 27 April 2022, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin used a structure-based machine-learning algorithm, an ensemble of three three-dimensional convolutional neural networks, to select stabilising mutations in a PET-hydrolysing enzyme, producing FAST-PETase. They reported that untreated post-consumer PET from 51 different thermoformed products was almost completely degraded within one week at 50 degrees Celsius and that the enzyme outperformed wild-type and engineered alternatives between 30 and 50 degrees Celsius; they closed the loop by resynthesising PET from the recovered monomers. An independent group at Texas A&M University, publishing in Environmental Science and Technology Letters on 19 March 2025, used FAST-PETase together with MHETase in a yeast whole-cell biocatalyst and reported complete depolymerisation of a PET film in seven days at 30 degrees Celsius.
purpose: Use a structure-based machine-learning model to predict stabilising mutations that make a PET hydrolase active and robust at moderate temperatures.
system: Structure-based machine-learning mutation predictor (ensemble of three 3D convolutional neural networks) applied to PETase engineering
developer: University of Texas at Austin (Alper and Ellington groups)
deployer: University of Texas at Austin; subsequently Texas A&M University

ratings.reason: A laboratory-scale enzyme that an independent group could pick up and reuse successfully; the sources report bench work, not production deployment.
Complete depolymerisation of untreated post-consumer PET was shown only in the laboratory in both the original and the independent study; neither source reports industrial-scale recycling.

ai_role.statement: The machine-learning model chose which mutations to introduce; the enzymatic activity was measured experimentally by the designers and later reproduced by a separate group at another institution that used FAST-PETase as a component of its own system.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the cited sources.

Corrected the temperature of the 51-product degradation experiment to 50 degrees Celsius (30 to 50 degrees Celsius is the range over which FAST-PETase outperformed alternatives, a different claim), credited the complete depolymerisation to FAST-PETase co-immobilised with MHETase rather than to FAST-PETase alone, and used the exact title of the ESTL paper.
